title: Reading Between the Lines
welcome_lead: Some meaning is on the page; some you must dig out.
meta_desc: KS3 English Language adventure on explicit and implicit meaning.
final_note: You can now tell explicit from implicit information in a text.

concepts.def: Reasoning from clues to a conclusion.

walkthroughs.body_html: 'Tom slammed the door' is explicit about an action; the anger behind it is implicit — we infer it.
Inference = reading between the lines. Use small clues to reach a fair conclusion the writer hasn't spelt out.
Always anchor inference in evidence — a quote or detail from the text. Without evidence, it's guesswork.

mcqs.q: What is a speech act according to Searle/Austin?
options: A speech act is any time someone speaks.
A speech act is a performance or a play.
An utterance that performs an action — promising, ordering, apologising, declaring. Speech acts have locutionary (what's said), illocutionary (intended force) and perlocutionary (effect) dimensions.
Language change only happens in informal speech, not in writing.

mcqs.q: Is language change a sign of decline?
options: Language change only happens in informal speech, not in writing.
Language change shows that standards are falling and English is being ruined.
No — modern linguistics treats change as natural and continuous, not as decay. Every language has always been changing and will continue to.
A speech act is a performance or a play.
A dialect that has gained social and institutional prestige — used in education and formal writing; it is one variety, not inherently superior in linguistic terms.
Language change only happens in informal speech, not in writing.
Standard English is the same as Received Pronunciation.
Standard English is the original and correct form of the language.
